A regular hexagon with side length 4 is subdivided into a lattice of 96 equilateral triangles of side length 1. Let $S$ be the set of all vertices of this lattice. Compute the number of nondegenerate triangles with vertices in $S$ that contain the center of the hexagon strictly in their interior.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let the triangular lattice be described by coordinates \((x,y)\) in two unit basis directions meeting at \(60^\circ\). The hexagon of side length \(4\) is

\[
\{(x,y)\in \mathbb Z^2:\ |x|\le 4,\ |y|\le 4,\ |x+y|\le 4\}.
\]

The center is \((0,0)\). The center itself cannot be a vertex of a triangle containing the center strictly in its interior, so we consider the \(60\) noncentral lattice vertices.

For three noncentral vertices, the center is strictly inside their triangle iff their three rays from the center are **not** contained in any closed half-plane through the center. Thus we only need to count choices of three rays satisfying this angular condition, weighted by how many lattice vertices lie on each ray.

A ray is determined by a primitive integer vector \((x,y)\). If

\[
L=\max(|x|,|y|,|x+y|),
\]

then that ray contains \(\lfloor 4/L\rfloor\) lattice vertices.

In the sector \(0^\circ \le \theta < 60^\circ\), the primitive vectors and their multiplicities are, in increasing angle,

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
(x,y) & L & \text{vertices on ray}\\ \hline
(1,0) & 1 & 4\\
(3,1) & 4 & 1\\
(2,1) & 3 & 1\\
(1,1) & 2 & 2\\
(1,2) & 3 & 1\\
(1,3) & 4 & 1
\end{array}
\]

So one \(60^\circ\) sector has ray weights

\[
4,1,1,2,1,1.
\]

By sixfold symmetry, there are \(36\) rays total, with weight sequence

\[
4,1,1,2,1,1
\]

repeated six times. Hence there are \(6\) rays of weight \(4\), \(6\) rays of weight \(2\), and \(24\) rays of weight \(1\). The total number of noncentral vertices is

\[
6\cdot 4+6\cdot 2+24=60.
\]

Let the ray weights be \(w_1,\dots,w_{36}\). A triangle whose center is strictly inside must use three distinct rays. The total number of choices from three distinct rays is the third elementary symmetric sum

\[
\sum_{i<j<k} w_iw_jw_k.
\]

We have

\[
W=\sum w_i=60,\qquad \sum w_i^2=144,\qquad \sum w_i^3=456.
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{i<j<k} w_iw_jw_k
=
\frac{W^3-3W\sum w_i^2+2\sum w_i^3}{6}
=
\frac{60^3-3\cdot 60\cdot 144+2\cdot 456}{6}
=
31832.
\]

Now subtract the ray triples that are contained in a closed semicircle.

Index the rays cyclically as \(0,1,\dots,35\). The ray opposite \(i\) is \(i+18\), and the open half-circle ahead of \(i\) contains exactly the next \(17\) rays.

A triple in an open semicircle is counted exactly once by its first ray after the complementary gap. For a block of \(17\) consecutive rays with total weight \(T\) and square-sum \(Q\), the weighted number of pairs in the block is

\[
\frac{T^2-Q}{2}.
\]

Using the period-\(6\) weight pattern, the values for \(i\bmod 6=0,1,2,3,4,5\) are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
i\bmod 6 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5\\ \hline
T & 26 & 29 & 29 & 28 & 29 & 29\\
Q & 56 & 71 & 71 & 68 & 71 & 71\\
\frac{T^2-Q}{2} & 310 & 385 & 385 & 358 & 385 & 385
\end{array}
\]

Thus the number of bad triples in open semicircles is

\[
6(310+385+385+358+385+385)=13248.
\]

It remains to subtract triples containing an opposite pair of rays. There are \(18\) opposite ray pairs: \(3\) of weight \(4\), \(3\) of weight \(2\), and \(12\) of weight \(1\). For an opposite pair of weight \(a\), the third ray may be any of the remaining \(60-2a\) vertices. Hence the number of such bad triples is

\[
3\cdot 4^2(60-2\cdot 4)+3\cdot 2^2(60-2\cdot 2)+12\cdot 1^2(60-2\cdot 1)
\]

\[
=3\cdot 16\cdot 52+3\cdot 4\cdot 56+12\cdot 1\cdot 58
=3864.
\]

Therefore the desired number is

\[
31832-13248-3864=14720.
\]

\[
\boxed{14720}
\]
